conventions.convention: The central product along α:Z₁→Z₂ is (G×H)/{(z,α(z)^{-1})}; the canonical images of z and α(z) are thereby identified.
A special p-group has Z(P)=P′=Φ(P) elementary abelian; an extraspecial p-group is additionally nonabelian and this common subgroup has order p.
The commutator pairing requires a chosen generator z of Z(P): [x,y]=z^{b_z(xZ(P),yZ(P))}; P/Z(P) is written multiplicatively while carrying its canonical F_p-vector-space structure.
For odd p, plus type means exponent p and minus type exponent p²; for p=2, plus and minus have respectively 2^{2n}+2^n and 2^{2n}-2^n solutions of x²=1, including the identity.
Cay(G,S) is the simple undirected graph with edges {g,gs} for s in (S∪S^{-1})\{e}; directions, labels, duplicate edges and identity loops are forgotten.
Graphs may have arbitrary vertex sets, but walks and paths are finite; a connected graph is required to be nonempty.
For a generating set S, word length minimizes over words in S∪S^{-1}, and d_S(g,h)=|g^{-1}h|_S; this metric is left invariant and need not be right invariant.
A quasi-isometric embedding uses λ≥1 and c≥0 in both inequalities; a coarse Lipschitz map allows A,B≥0.

A quasi-isometry is a coarse Lipschitz map admitting a coarse Lipschitz quasi-inverse whose composites are at bounded distance from the identities; its equivalence with a coarsely dense quasi-isometric embedding is stated under the Axiom of Choice.
A dinatural transformation α:P→Q has components α_c:P(c,c)→Q(c,c) satisfying Q(1_c,f)α_cP(f,1_c)=Q(f,1_{c′})α_{c′}P(1_{c′},f).
A subscripted integral denotes an end and a superscripted integral a coend; an end is a terminal wedge and a coend an initial cowedge, and neither is assumed to exist.

Tw(C) has arrows f:c→c′ as objects and morphisms f→g given by pairs (a,b) with bfa=g; its projection sends f to (c,c′). An end is a limit over Tw(C), whereas a coend is a colimit over Tw(C)^op with domain and codomain interchanged.
For Set-weighted limits the weight is covariant W:J→Set; for weighted colimits it is a presheaf W:J^op→Set.
For a presheaf W, a morphism (c,x)→(d,y) in its category of elements lies over f:c→d and satisfies x=W(f)(y); the weighted colimit is taken over this category without another opposite.

load_bearing.statement: For T:C^op×C→D, an end is a terminal object of the category of wedges over T, and a coend is an initial object of the category of cowedges under T. Neither need exist.
For a finite p-group P the following are equivalent: P is extraspecial; P is nonabelian, |Z(P)|=p and P/Z(P) is elementary abelian; P is nonabelian and Z(P)=P′=Φ(P) has order p.
For a group G generated by S, the word metric is d_S(g,h)=|g^{-1}h|_S.
For T:C^op×C→D, a wedge from d to T is a dinatural transformation Δd→T, and a cowedge from T to d is a dinatural transformation T→Δd; their morphisms commute with every component.
A map f:X→Y is coarse Lipschitz if d_Y(fx,fx′)≤A d_X(x,x′)+B for some A,B≥0; it is a quasi-isometric embedding if λ^{-1}d_X(x,x′)−c≤d_Y(fx,fx′)≤λd_X(x,x′)+c for some λ≥1,c≥0.
Cay(G,S) is the simple graph with vertex set G and edge set {{g,gs}:g∈G, s∈(S∪S^{-1})\{e}}.

A subset A⊆Y is coarsely dense when every point of Y lies within one uniform bound of A. A quasi-isometry is a coarse Lipschitz map admitting a coarse Lipschitz quasi-inverse, with both composites at bounded distance from the appropriate identity.
For extraspecial P with a chosen generator z of Z(P), b_z:P/Z(P)×P/Z(P)→F_p is determined by [x,y]=z^{b_z(xZ(P),yZ(P))}.
For central subgroups Z₁≤Z(G), Z₂≤Z(H) and an isomorphism α:Z₁→Z₂, G∘_αH=(G×H)/{(z,α(z)^{-1}):z∈Z₁}.
For small J, locally small M and D:J→M, a limit weight is W:J→Set and {W,D} represents m↦Nat(W,M(m,D−)); a colimit weight is W:J^op→Set and W⋆D represents m↦Nat(W,M(D−,m)).

concerns.concern: The second Remark says the signs multiply under central products and cites the odd-prime absorption lemma. Under this item's odd-p convention M_p is minus, while M_p∘M_p≅M_p∘H_p still has exponent p² and is minus. Thus minus central-product minus is minus here, not plus.

Fact [L17] attributes to def-plus-and-minus-type-of-an-extraspecial-p-group the claim that a 2-group is plus exactly when it is a central product of dihedral factors. The cited Definition instead fixes 2-type by the two counts of solutions to x²=1. Step 6 cites [L17], so the dependency restatement is inaccurate even though [L4] supplies the count-based fact needed.

Connected graphs, and hence trees, are defined to be nonempty. The empty simple graph is not a tree, but the Statement's condition on each pair of vertices is vacuously true. The iff needs a nonempty hypothesis or a nonvacuous formulation.
The Statement does not quantify two connected simple graphs. The path metric is defined only for connected simple graphs, so the claim is not well formed at its stated generality.

The title says finite generating set, but the Statement drops the generating hypothesis. For a subset that does not generate the group, the Cayley graph is disconnected while this page's path metric is defined only for connected graphs, so “the two distances agree” is not defined as written.

Step 1.1 chooses a finite left transversal, but step 3.1 uses g=r(g)t(g) with r(g)∈H, which requires a right transversal. Replacing “left” by “right”, or inverting the transversal, repairs the Schreier argument immediately.

Steps 1.3 and 4.1 need the peeled-factor isomorphisms to be compatible on their common centres. The proof establishes C≅C′ and that the peeled factors are H_p, but does not state that an automorphism of H_p realizes any automorphism of its order-p centre. An explicit scaling automorphism closes the gap.
Step 1.2 says g_{j+1}g_j^{-1} along a right Cayley edge is a basis letter. From g_{j+1}=g_js_j, the basis letter is g_j^{-1}g_{j+1}=s_j. Reversing the quotient repairs the argument.

The converse proves only that a quasi-isometry has coarsely dense image. It omits the standard lower quasi-isometric-embedding estimate derived from a coarse Lipschitz quasi-inverse and bounded distance of gf from the identity.
For f:R→R, step 1.1 calls the inclusion 2Z→R a quasi-inverse, but a quasi-inverse must have domain all of R. Taking g=id_R gives gf=f and fg=f, both uniformly within 2 of the identity.
The first Remark contains a stray proof-ending symbol in “the form taken ∎ above” inside a definition item.
